title: Carrying someone’s bags
description: A short guide to the oldest offer of help there is, and how to make it easy to accept.

body.heading: Offer to the hands, not the person
paragraphs: “Those look heavy — may I take one?” works better than “Do you need help?” The first offers a specific relief; the second asks someone to declare themselves incapable in public. Specific, small offers are dramatically easier to accept.
Point the offer at a visible load: the bag, the box, the pushchair versus the stairs. You are not rescuing anyone. You are redistributing weight, which is the most ordinary kindness in the world.

body.heading: Take no gracefully
paragraphs: Some people will decline — from pride, habit, or a perfectly good system of their own. Accept it with a smile and no second push. Help that must be accepted is not help; it is a performance with a captive audience.
A declined offer still does its work. The person now knows the offer exists in the world, and your corner of it is a friendlier place than it was a minute ago.

body.heading: Carry it all the way
paragraphs: If the offer is accepted, finish the job: to the car, to the door, to the top of the stairs — not to the convenient halfway point where your enthusiasm ran out. Half-carried help teaches people not to accept help, and the lesson is hard to un-teach.
Then hand it back without ceremony and be gone. The dignity is in the lightness of the whole transaction.

takeaway: Offer specifically, accept refusal lightly, and carry what you carry all the way.
